strengths: Significance: Treating images as discretized, randomly deformed functions provides a useful framework for separating image resolution from ambient input dimension. The distinction between deformation variability and label noise motivates worthwhile theoretical questions.

Originality: The most interesting contribution is the joint analysis of resolution, template separation, and deformation complexity. The alignment classifier and constructive CNN representation offer complementary ways to study invariance, even though registration and deformation-based modeling themselves are established ideas.

Presentation: The manuscript explains the generative model and classifier constructions accessibly, provides illustrative figures, and includes extensive proofs. The specialized alignment result in Theorem 3.6 offers a concrete account of why one example per class can suffice under strong structural assumptions.

Limitations and ethics: The authors explicitly acknowledge computationally intractable 0–1 optimization and discuss background noise, partial visibility, and multiple templates as extensions. These are appropriate qualifications. The theoretical setting and MNIST experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 4.1 is false for the estimator actually defined. Equation (27) minimizes −(1/n)∑ k_i 1(q_2(X_i)>1/2), which rewards positive predictions on class 1 but never penalizes false positives. A network that always predicts class 1 is therefore a global minimizer, with population error 1−π even as n grows. Equation (94) explicitly, and incorrectly, equates this objective with empirical misclassification risk. Replacing the objective by the actual 0–1 loss may repair this issue, but the central learning guarantee does not hold as written.

Soundness—The proof of Theorem 3.1 contains a substantive quantifier error. Lemma A.3 establishes closeness to the normalized template for an approximately correct inverse B*. On page 29, the proof applies that bound to arbitrary B_i and B in the inverse covering when excluding wrong-class matches. Arbitrary inverse candidates need not undo the generating deformation. Since classifier (10) minimizes over all such candidates, existence of good inverses cannot establish the required uniform lower bound for wrong-class distances. A new argument or stronger assumptions are needed.

Soundness—The claimed optimal separation threshold is not established by Theorem 3.7. That theorem constructs indistinguishable pixel arrays with raw L2 template distance of order 1/d, whereas the upper bounds use normalized distance minimized over deformations, D in (12) or (21). A lower bound on raw distance does not imply a lower bound on D. The construction must control separation after optimizing over transformations before it can justify the repeated claim that the proposed separation condition is optimal. The theorem's quantifiers also obscure that its constructed alternative template depends on d.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Section 5 omits the deformation ranges, training epochs, batch size, loss used for CNN training, and sufficient details to recreate template selection and preprocessing. Figure 8 reports medians across 30 repetitions with only 100 test images per repetition, without uncertainty intervals. The experimental CNNs use small filters and local pooling, unlike the analyzed architecture with global max-pooling and a deformation-dependent filter bank. With resolution fixed at 28×28 and no controlled separation or deformation-complexity sweeps, the experiments illustrate the alignment heuristic but do not validate the central theoretical rates.

Significance and originality are narrower than the framing suggests. Under the model, noiseless images come from two fixed template families with assumed separation. The CNN result uses an exhaustive deformation-specific filter construction followed by a standard realizable VC bound; with |A_d| of order d² or d³, the sample bound scales as d⁴/n or d⁶/n up to logarithms. This is potentially useful specialized theory, but it provides limited support for broader explanations of practical CNN performance. The manuscript should distinguish its new statistical results more sharply from existing template matching, registration, scattering, and invariant-network work.

Presentation and technical consistency need improvement. Theorem 4.2, Lemma 4.3, and Proposition B.4 refer to separation (21), which concerns axis-aligned scaling and translation, although their general-deformation proofs use (12). Equations (2) and (15) omit the d² pixel-average factor used elsewhere, including in their proofs. These inconsistencies make it difficult to determine precisely which statements are intended. Together with the two central proof problems, they prevent the manuscript from being a reliable foundation in its current form.

strengths: Significance: Modeling images as pixel averages of randomly deformed templates provides a useful setting for studying how resolution, invariance, and sample size interact. The distinction between additional pixels and additional independent covariates is valuable.

Originality: Although deformation models and invariant matching are established ideas, connecting discretization error, template separation, and CNN classification guarantees is a potentially useful theoretical contribution.

Presentation: The manuscript explains the model and alignment algorithm accessibly, illustrates the constructions, and supplies extensive proofs. Its discussion explicitly acknowledges computationally intractable optimization and extensions beyond the analyzed setting.

Limitations and ethics: The authors acknowledge background noise, partial visibility, and multiple templates as limitations or extensions. These are appropriate disclosures, and the theoretical work and MNIST experiments raise no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—The CNN estimator is not an empirical misclassification minimizer. Equation (27) minimizes −Σ k_i 1(q_2(X_i)>1/2), which rewards positive predictions on class 1 but never penalizes false positives. A constant classifier predicting 1 is therefore a global minimizer for every dataset, yet has population error 1−π. This contradicts Theorem 4.1's vanishing bound. Appendix B repeats the problem by asserting an incorrect equivalence between this objective and empirical 0–1 loss immediately after Lemma B.8. Replacing the objective may repair this component, but the central theorem is false as currently stated.

Soundness—The proof of Theorem 3.1 contains a separate, substantive quantifier error. Lemma A.3 establishes closeness to the normalized template for an appropriately chosen approximate inverse B*. On page 29, the proof applies that bound to arbitrary B_i and B in the inverse cover to lower-bound every cross-class comparison. Arbitrary inverse candidates need not undo the actual deformation. Since classifier (10) minimizes over all candidates, existence of good inverses does not establish the required uniform cross-class separation. The general perfect-classification guarantee is therefore unsupported by the supplied proof.

Soundness—The claimed optimality of the separation condition is not established in the stated metric. Theorem 3.7 constructs indistinguishable images with raw L2 template distance of order 1/d, whereas the upper bounds use normalized distance minimized over transformations, D in (12) or (21). A lower bound on raw distance does not imply a lower bound on this transformation-minimized distance. The construction is informative about pixelization ambiguity, but additional analysis is needed to claim a matching lower bound for D.

Significance and empirical support: Section 5 compares alignment against three CNNs on deformations of one or ten MNIST templates per class, at a single resolution, d=28. The experimental CNNs differ from the theoretical architecture and are trained with Adam rather than the analyzed global optimization procedure. These experiments illustrate the alignment method's advantage in a favorable setting, but do not validate the resolution-dependent separation thresholds or CNN learning rate. In particular, the bound scales approximately as d^4/n for scaling deformations, before logarithmic factors; it does not substantiate the text's suggestion that tiny training sets should suffice for CNNs.

Reproducibility: Section 5 gives architectures, optimizer, learning rate, test size, and repetition count, but omits deformation ranges, training loss, epochs, batch size, template identifiers, and random seeds. No implementation link is provided. Figure 8 reports medians over 30 repetitions without variability, making the stability of the comparisons difficult to assess.

Presentation and positioning: The broad novelty claims need sharper qualification against the cited pattern-theory, registration, scattering, and functional-classification literature. Describing conventional classification as treating pixels as independent variables is misleading: using pixels as covariates does not require independence. There are also consequential inconsistencies, including Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.3 referring to the specialized separation quantity (21) while discussing the general deformation model.

strengths: Significance: Modeling images as pixel averages of randomly deformed templates provides a useful setting for studying resolution, invariance, and classification jointly. The distinction between increasing resolution and increasing unconstrained input dimension is conceptually valuable.

Originality: Although deformation models and invariant template matching have substantial precedents acknowledged by the paper, the resolution-dependent separation analysis and its connection to CNN generalization offer a potentially useful theoretical contribution.

Methodology: The explicit image-alignment classifier and construction of CNN filters from discretized template deformations provide interpretable mechanisms for handling nuisance variation. The MNIST-derived experiments illustrate the alignment classifier's effectiveness with very few examples.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript explains the model intuitively, provides extensive proofs, and openly discusses computationally intractable optimization, background noise, partial visibility, and multiple templates. These acknowledgments appropriately delineate the intended prototype setting. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect CNN objective: Equation (27) minimizes minus the number of correctly predicted positive examples, not empirical misclassification error. It never penalizes false positives. Consequently, a network predicting class 1 everywhere is always a minimizer, but has population error 1−π, contradicting Theorem 4.1's vanishing bound for fixed resolution. Equation (94) explicitly asserts an invalid equivalence between this objective and 0–1 empirical risk, so the problem propagates into the proof. Replacing the objective with actual misclassification loss may repair this issue, but the central theorem is false for the estimator currently defined.

Soundness—gap in Theorem 3.1: Lemma A.3 establishes proximity to the normalized template for an appropriately chosen approximate inverse B*. The proof of Theorem 3.1, on pages 28–29, then uses that bound for arbitrary B and Bi when lower-bounding distances between different classes. Arbitrary inverse candidates need not undo the actual deformations. Because classifier (10) minimizes over all such candidates, controlling only the correctly aligned candidates is insufficient. A uniform cross-class separation argument, potentially with additional assumptions, is needed.

Soundness—optimality is overstated: Theorem 3.7 constructs indistinguishable pixel observations with untransformed L2 template distance of order 1/d. It does not establish a corresponding lower bound for the deformation-minimized, normalized separation D used in Theorems 3.1 and 3.6. Thus it demonstrates a discretization obstruction, but does not by itself establish the claimed matching necessity for that separation criterion.

Presentation and specification: Theorem 4.1 uses separation (12), whereas Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.3 reference (21), which only describes scaling and translation. Proposition B.4 likewise states (21) but its proof uses (12). These are materially different definitions for general deformation classes and must be reconciled.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Section 5 reports only fixed-resolution, synthetically transformed MNIST examples, with 100 test images and medians over 30 repetitions. It does not test resolution-dependent separation rates, rotation/nonlinear-deformation guarantees, or the theoretical CNN architecture and optimization rule. Transformation ranges, training epochs, batch sizes, training loss, template identifiers, and uncertainty estimates are missing, and no code availability statement is provided. The experiments therefore offer limited validation and are difficult to reproduce faithfully.

Significance and scope: The guarantees concern noiseless, fully visible objects generated from one template per class, with an explicit separation condition. Even after correcting the theoretical issues, the CNN bound requires sample sizes exceeding approximately the architecture's parameter count and does not explain practical optimization or performance with few examples. This remains a worthwhile specialized direction, but the unresolved errors in central results prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality: The useful contribution is the resolution-dependent statistical analysis of deformation-based classification, rather than deformation modeling itself. Treating pixels as local averages of continuous templates gives a meaningful way to distinguish increasing image resolution from increasing ambient dimension.

Technical contribution: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 provide explicit sufficient conditions for perfect classification with one example per class. The CNN construction connects approximation by deformation-specific filters with statistical complexity bounds for both 0–1 and clipped cross-entropy empirical risk minimization.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript explains the classifiers intuitively, supplies extensive proofs, and discusses connections to registration, functional data analysis, and scattering transforms. It explicitly acknowledges computationally expensive inverse matching, idealized optimization, background noise, occlusion, and sharp boundaries. These acknowledgments are appropriate.

Significance: The framework could provide a useful theoretical benchmark for separating geometric variability from label uncertainty. The synthetic experiments illustrate that alignment can be effective with very few examples under the assumed template model. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—claimed optimal separation is not established: Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between two templates producing identical pixels. The sufficient conditions instead use distances minimized over transformations and brightness, as in (12) and (23). A lower bound before minimization does not establish a lower bound afterward. The proof does not show that its constructed templates have deformation-invariant separation of order 1/d, so the repeated claim that it proves optimality of the proposed separation criterion is unsupported. The construction also depends on d, although the theorem's quantifier order suggests fixed templates working for every sufficiently large d.

Soundness—the noninvertible CNN setting needs stronger assumptions or a revised proof: Assumption 2-(i) requires the template-support rectangle to lie inside A([0,1]^2). Without injectivity, this does not imply that the support of f composed with A lies inside [0,1]^2: points outside the image can also map into the template support. Nevertheless, Proposition B.4 explicitly uses this implication, and the CNN argument uses whole-plane separation and compact-support identities. Section 4 specifically claims that invertibility is unnecessary. An explicit preimage-support condition and corresponding proof are needed to justify that generality.

Soundness—additional theoretical claims overreach: The statement following Theorem 4.4 that the V/n rate is minimax optimal cites a general VC-class result, but supplies no lower bound for the restricted deformation-generated distributions. Indeed, Section 3 gives perfect classification from one example per class under its conditions. Also, the proposed route to 1/d CNN separation on pp. 20–21 temporarily ignores global maximization over shifts, which is a substantive architectural issue rather than an established extension.

Evaluation and significance: The experiments use deformations of selected individual templates from named datasets, not classification across their natural within-class variation. This is appropriate for illustrating the model, but provides limited evidence for broader image-classification claims. They do not vary resolution or template separation to test the central theoretical predictions, and Figure 11 reports only median errors on 200 test examples over ten repetitions, without dispersion. The fixed 10×10-filter networks trained with Adam are not shown to implement the analyzed block-structured, bounded-weight, clipped-output ERM setting, so declining empirical error does not validate the stated rates.

Reproducibility: Section 5 and Appendix C omit important experimental details, including deformation distributions and ranges, exact template identifiers, background-removal procedures, complete network depth and pooling specifications, training epochs, batch sizes, and stopping criteria. No code availability statement is provided. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction of the numerical results.

Presentation and positioning: The discussion on pp. 19–20 characterizes prior generalization bounds, including spectrally normalized margin bounds, as applying only to functions independent of training data. Uniform generalization bounds can apply to data-dependent learned predictors; the presence of an empirical-loss term does not imply otherwise. The distinction should instead emphasize the manuscript's explicit approximation construction under a particular generative model. The lengthy exposition would also benefit from a compact comparison of assumptions, separation quantities, and guarantees across the three methods.

strengths: Significance: Modeling pixels as averages of a deformed continuous template provides a useful setting for studying how image resolution and geometric variability affect classification. The distinction between increasing resolution and increasing an unstructured input dimension is valuable.

Technical contribution: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give explicit sufficient separation conditions for perfect classification using one example per class. The CNN approximation construction and subsequent bounds for both 0–1 and cross-entropy empirical risk minimization constitute substantial theoretical work.

Originality: Although template deformation and registration are established ideas, connecting pixel discretization, deformation-class complexity, and CNN classification guarantees offers a potentially useful contribution in statistical understanding.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript provides extensive proofs, helpful illustrations, and connections to functional data analysis and scattering transforms. It explicitly acknowledges computationally demanding inverse searches, idealized optimization, and difficulties involving backgrounds, occlusion, and sharp edges. I identified no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—separation optimality is not established as claimed. The sufficient conditions use deformation-invariant distances D in equations (12) and (23), whereas Theorem 3.8 only lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between two templates producing identical pixels. A lower bound before minimizing over transformations does not imply a lower bound afterward. The proof in Appendix A.2 does not supply the missing bound on D, so the claims that the proposed separation criterion is necessary or optimal are unsupported. Additionally, the theorem places the existence of the templates before 'for any d', while its construction depends on d; this quantification needs correction.

Soundness—the minimax interpretation of the CNN rate is overstated. Following Theorem 4.4, the manuscript calls V/n minimax optimal by citing a general VC-class result. That does not establish a matching lower bound for this restricted template-deformation distribution family. Indeed, Section 3 shows that suitable classifiers can succeed once both labels have appeared. The paper needs a model-specific lower bound or a clearly qualified statement about generic learning bounds.

Presentation and positioning: Pages 19–20 incorrectly characterize the cited neural-network generalization literature, including the spectrally normalized margin bounds of Bartlett et al., as concerning functions that cannot depend on training data. Uniform generalization bounds can apply to learned predictors. The genuine distinction here is the explicit approximation analysis under a generative model, not an inability of earlier bounds to accommodate data-dependent learning.

Significance and empirical support: Section 5 generates training and test examples by deforming individual source templates. These are controlled synthetic recognition tasks using images taken from named datasets, rather than evaluations of generalization across distinct objects within those datasets. This is appropriate for illustrating the model, but the experiments do not test the principal resolution-dependent separation predictions, nonlinear deformation complexity, or robustness beyond the model. Increasing sample size and observing declining error provides only weak corroboration of the specific theoretical rates.

Reproducibility and uncertainty: The experiments omit deformation distributions and ranges, source-image identifiers, detailed background preprocessing, training epochs, batch size, and complete network specifications. No code link is supplied. Figures 9 and 11 report medians over ten repetitions with only 50 or 200 test examples and no variability estimates; zero median error at those sample sizes does not substantiate perfect population classification.

Theory-to-experiment connection: The CNN theorems concern global empirical risk minimizers over specifically constrained architectures, including bounded parameters, block-structured filters, and clipped outputs for cross-entropy. The experiments use Adam and fixed 10-by-10 filters without explaining how the remaining theoretical constraints are implemented. The optimization limitation is honestly acknowledged, but the reported experiments cannot establish that these guarantees describe the trained networks. Overall, the useful theoretical framework does not outweigh the unresolved optimality claims and incomplete empirical specification.

strengths: Originality: The useful contribution is the statistical analysis of deformation-generated images, particularly the connection between pixel resolution, template separation, and deformation complexity. This provides new understanding beyond simply proposing an invariant classifier.

Significance: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 identify conditions under which one example per class suffices after registration or alignment. The CNN construction offers a complementary account of how filters can represent different deformations.

Presentation: The manuscript explains the generative model and classifiers clearly, illustrates their operation, and supplies extensive proofs. Its discussion of registration, functional data analysis, and scattering transforms provides helpful context.

Limitations and ethics: The authors explicitly discuss ideal optimization, background noise, occlusion, and sharp edges. These acknowledgments appropriately delimit the intended setting. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The generality claimed for the CNN results is not supported by the stated assumptions. Assumption 2(i) requires the template support rectangle to lie inside A([0,1]^2), but for noninvertible A this does not ensure that the support of f composed with A lies inside [0,1]^2: additional preimages can occur outside the image. Nevertheless, Proposition B.4 and Proposition B.5 use precisely this support property, including when relating whole-plane separation to observed-image correlations. Equation (90) also uses a change-of-variables equality without accounting for multiplicity. Theorems 4.1–4.4 need stronger assumptions or revised proofs, especially given the explicit claim that invertibility is unnecessary.

Soundness of optimality claims: Theorem 3.8 establishes indistinguishable pixel observations for templates separated in ordinary normalized L2 distance. It does not establish a lower bound on the deformation-invariant separation D used in Theorems 3.1 and 3.7. Because D minimizes over transformations and brightness, ordinary L2 separation does not imply comparable D-separation. Consequently, the claimed matching necessity of the D ≳ 1/d condition remains unproved. Likewise, a generic VC-class lower bound does not establish minimax optimality over this restricted deformation-generated distribution family.

Empirical support and significance: Section 5 uses synthetic deformations of fixed template images drawn from named datasets, rather than classification across different natural instances. This is a reasonable model sanity check, but does not establish broader object-recognition performance. The experiments also do not vary resolution or template separation to test the central theoretical scaling claims. Medians over 10 repetitions, with only 50 or 200 test examples and no uncertainty intervals, provide limited evidence for near-zero error.

Reproducibility: The manuscript gives filter sizes, widths, optimizer, and learning rate, but omits important details including deformation distributions and ranges, exact template identifiers, background-removal procedures, training epochs, batch sizes, and complete network specifications. No code availability statement is provided. The experiments also do not document enforcement of the bounded weights, filter block structure, or clipped probabilities used in the theory.

Positioning: Pages 19–20 characterize cited generalization bounds, including Bartlett et al. [8], as applying only to functions independent of training data. Uniform generalization bounds can apply to data-dependent learned predictors; an empirical-loss term does not imply otherwise. The defensible distinction is the paper's explicit approximation construction and distribution-specific risk analysis. This comparison should be corrected.
